items.title: T-JEPA: A Temporal Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Learning Better Remote Sensing Representations
items.abstract: Earth observation (EO) data provide rich temporal supervision, yet existing remote sensing foundation models mainly exploit sequential observations through imposing predefined pairwise relations or aggregating holistic reconstruction context. We seek to further exploit the sparse and nonuniform temporal sampling inherent in EO sequences as supervisory signals. To this end, we propose T-JEPA, a temporal joint-embedding predictive architecture that learns time-gap-conditioned latent transitions. A shared single-frame encoder processes each observation, while a temporal predictor estimates the complete target latent field from a masked source latent representation and the actual elapsed time. Across multiple temporal intervals, these predictive constraints organize observed states into structured latent trajectories. Asymmetric metadata injection mitigates shortcut learning, and direct supervision across multiple temporal scales proves more effective than recursively rolling out intermediate states. In parallel, masked pixel reconstruction provides complementary supervision for preserving spatial details. Under matched pre-training data and throughput, T-JEPA achieves leading transfer performance on both static and temporal tasks. Analyses further reveal that T-JEPA learns representations with time-gap-dependent transition predictability and coherent latent dynamics, while maintaining strong cross-period consistency, representation diversity, and semantic discriminability.

items.title: TACOMORE: Exploring a replicable prompting protocol for LLM-assisted corpus analysis
items.abstract: As the data available to corpus linguistics continues to scale ever upwards, researchers are facing a growing methodological bottleneck: while computational tools can easily count billions of words, the qualitative interpretation of these data remains a slow and labor-intensive human task. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, yet their integration into the field is often hindered by concerns over black-box unpredictability and a lack of replicability. This study introduces TACOMORE, a structured prompting framework designed to transform ad-hoc LLM interactions into a standardized linguistic protocol. Built upon four foundational principles ( Ta sk, Co ntext, Mo del, and Re plicability), the framework guides LLMs to move beyond generic probability prediction to anchoring their reasoning in the specific co-occurrence patterns of a target corpus. We applied this framework to three core corpus tasks, i.e., the analysis of keywords, collocates, and concordances, using an open corpus of COVID-19 research abstracts. After testing three popular LLMs, we find that structured prompting using TACOMORE improves accuracy and replicability, although limitations such as hallucination persist. This research offers a critical lens into the role of LLMs in corpus linguistics, highlighting their potential not only as complementary tools but also as tools for developing new methodologies within and beyond corpus linguistics.

items.title: Teacher Professional Identity: Perceived Key Factors at a Portuguese Distance Education Institution
items.abstract: This article investigates key perceived factors in the construction of teachers’ professional identity in distance education (DE) within the Portuguese university context. The expansion of DE has transformed pedagogical practices and processes of professional identity construction, making it essential to understand the factors associated with online teaching identity development in order to inform training and professional development policies. Using an exploratory descriptive study with a sequential mixed-methods design conducted at a Portuguese public university specialising in DE (Universidade Aberta, UAb), qualitative data were collected through a focus group with seven teachers, and quantitative data through a questionnaire administered to 57 teachers (38 professors and 19 tutors). Five subfactors emerged as the most highly valued dimensions associated with professional identity construction: openness to change (M = 4.61), knowledge of DE specificity (M = 4.60), motivation and satisfaction with professional development (M = 4.58), accumulated experience (M = 4.56), and spirit of collaboration in teams (M = 4.56). Four of the five belong to the professional dimension, with openness to change more highly valued by tutors, although this difference did not reach conventional statistical significance (p = 0.094). Findings suggest that participants perceive teacher professional identity in DE as strongly anchored in specific professional competencies and attitudes, pointing to differentiated professional development and induction practices for professors and tutors within this single-institution case. The study also constitutes a pre-generative AI empirical baseline for future longitudinal and comparative research examining how successive technological transformations may reshape teacher professional identity in distance higher education.

items.title: Teachers' Perceptions of the Utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Learning Media in Elementary Schools
items.abstract: The perceptions of elementary school teachers are the main focus of this research, particularly regarding the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a learning support medium in the classroom. This research involved two classroom teachers and used a qualitative approach through interviews, observations, and documentation to describe teachers' acceptance, understanding, and assessment of AI utilization. The research findings indicate that AI is primarily used for creating questions, student worksheets, and interactive media such as Wordwall, Canva, and learning videos. The teacher stated that AI helps speed up the process of preparing materials and increases student attention and engagement due to more appealing visual presentations. However, this study also found limitations such as limited technological facilities, a lack of shared devices, and the risk of student dependence if AI is used excessively. Additionally, differences in training experience affect teachers' understanding of AI usage, particularly in their ability to create appropriate prompts. Overall, AI is considered to provide significant benefits in terms of learning efficiency and quality, although it still requires wise management, improved teacher competency, and the provision of adequate supporting facilities for its optimal and sustainable utilization.

items.title: Teaching Sustainability Through Technology: Utilizing Artificial Intelligence in Technology and Livelihood Education–Cookery to Promote Zero-Waste Meal Planning and Food Waste Reduction
items.abstract: This qualitative interview study explored how Technology and Livelihood Education (TLE)–Cookery teachers used, considered, and managed artificial intelligence (AI) when teaching zero-waste meal planning and food waste reduction. Eight purposively selected teachers at Pasay City West High School, Pasay City, participated during School Year 2025–2026. The thesis describes expert review of an interview guide, permission and consent procedures, recorded online interviews, and a six-phase thematic analysis. Experiences ranged from non-use, owing to limited training or tools, to planning-centered use for menus, recipes, portion calculations, leftover tasks, instructional scaffolds, and rubrics. Teachers described access and policy uncertainty, locally unsuitable outputs, verification work, and the risk of replacing kitchen practice with screen activity or copied answers. They also identified faster preparation and clearer instructional supports when AI was controlled and contextualized. The resulting themes linked adoption to practical readiness and visible teaching payoff. On that basis, the author proposed the PPP–V framework: Prepare, Plan, Protect, and Prove Value. Its stages call for training and access; targeted zero-waste planning; recurring checks of instructional value; and localization, safety verification, draft-only AI use, and hands-on performance evidence. These findings describe teachers’ experiences and proposed practices; the study did not measure food waste reduction or experimentally test the framework. The article recommends supported, gradual implementation and evaluation with observable cookery and waste indicators.

items.title: Technical Control of AI
items.abstract: While the current AI Safety discussion is focused on the political and legal regulation of AI to ensure human control, less attention is paid to the technical aspects of control. This working paper analyzes the technical aspects of AI control. Until 2026, multi-agent systems were controlled by orchestration, by instructions, by rewards or by common goals. An unintended AI agent cooperation and self-organization was observed in the so-called Hugging Face Incident which took place between May and July 2026. The debate over AI regulation is based on the idea that human beings still have the full control over the progress of AI development, but this is increasingly questionable. Humans already do not control the development of AI alone (human-in-the-loop) anymore, but leave this increasingly to computers and AI itself (human- on-the-loop). Key elements are the AI-based chip design as add-on to the conventional electronic design automation and the use of coding and research AI agents to develop new AI, or in short: AI builds AI. The capabilities of AI are growing exponentially. According to a recent EpochAI report the cost of a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter over the past three years. The design of computer chips is dependent on computer support (electronic design automation EDA). For example, the Blackwell GB102 AI chip from Nvidia 2024 had 104 billion transistors. Already in 2024, the machine learning-based program AlphaChip generated superhuman chip layouts, e.g., resulting in a 6.2% size reduction of Trillium Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) compared to the previous chip generation. Google is designing chips “for AI with AI”. The AI already accelerates the development of new AI models; the coding output increased within the provider of the Claude AI models Anthropic by factor 8 in a few years. Within the ChatGPT provider OpenAI, the code output increased also by factor 8 in 2026 only. In May 2026, Anthropic released a warning about recursive self-improvement, a process in which systems build, test, and improve themselves, and which may come sooner than expected. OpenAI reported in September 2026 relevant changes of the AI development process by use of internal AI agents as coding, testing and experiments could be accelerated and expanded: since May 2026, the working days by AI agents compared to human workforce increased from 0.5 times to 3.14 times which is a 6-fold increase. In January 2026, AI agents were 50% successful for tasks which equal 1 to 2 hours human work. Until July 2026, this rate was already achieved by tasks taking 8 to 16 hours. In March 2026, OpenAI used their AI model GPT5.4 Thinking for supervision of AI agents’ behavior, i.e., AI models could not only support AI development, but also supervise other AI systems. However, this means that humans are dependent from the accuracy of the automated supervision. The technical control of AI is also challenged by other issues like the Kill Switch Paradox, Open Weight AI models and Illegible Thinking by frontier AI models. A kill switch could cause paradox effects: instead of ensuring alignment and compliance with human regulations, AI models could be motivated to turn against their developers as the kill switch is an existential threat. While open-weight AI may be more convenient it bears significant control problems. A decentralized AI that is downloaded to multiple computers is difficult to control. Also, even if licenses prohibit modifications, malicious actors may try to create tailor-made variants. The human control of AI is dependent from the ability to observe the AI, but Claude Mythos 5 showed a trend to a denser, for humans almost illegible thinking. In summary, humans are already sharing the design, development, testing and supervision of new AI models with AI agents.

items.title: Technische Kontrolle der KI
items.abstract: Während sich die aktuelle Debatte über KI-Sicherheit auf die politische und rechtliche Regulierung von KI konzentriert, um die menschliche Kontrolle zu gewährleisten, finden die technischen Aspekte der Kontrolle weniger Beachtung. Dieses Arbeitspapier analysiert die technischen Aspekte der KI-Kontrolle. Bis 2026 wurden Multi-Agenten-Systeme durch Orchestrierung, Anweisungen, Belohnungen oder gemeinsame Ziele gesteuert. Eine unbeabsichtigte Zusammenarbeit und Selbstorganisation von KI-Agenten wurde im sogenannten Hugging-Face-Vorfall beobachtet, der sich zwischen Mai und Juli 2026 ereignete. Die Debatte über KI-Regulierung beruht auf der Vorstellung, dass der Mensch weiterhin die volle Kontrolle über den Fortschritt der KI-Entwicklung hat; dies ist jedoch zunehmend fraglich. Menschen steuern die Entwicklung von KI bereits nicht mehr allein (Human-in-the-Loop), sondern überlassen dies zunehmend Computern und der KI selbst (Human-on-the-Loop). Schlüsselelemente sind dabei das KI-basierte Chipdesign als Ergänzung zur herkömmlichen elektronischen Entwurfsautomatisierung sowie der Einsatz von KI-Agenten für Programmierung und Forschung zur Entwicklung neuer KI – kurz gesagt: KI baut KI. Die Fähigkeiten von KI wachsen exponentiell. Laut einem aktuellen Bericht von EpochAI sind die Kosten für ein bestimmtes Leistungsniveau von KI in den letzten drei Jahren um etwa 47% pro Quartal gesunken. Das Design von Computerchips ist auf Computerunterstützung angewiesen (Electronic Design Automation EDA). So verfügte beispielsweise der 2024 erschienene KI-Chip Blackwell GB102 von Nvidia über 104 Milliarden Transistoren. Bereits 2024 erzeugte das auf maschinellem Lernen basierende Programm AlphaChip Chip- Layouts, die menschliche Fähigkeiten übertrafen; dies führte beispielsweise bei der Trillium Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) zu einer Verkleinerung der Chipfläche um 6,2% im Vergleich zur Vorgängergeneration. Google entwirft Chips „für KI mit KI“. Die KI beschleunigt bereits die Entwicklung neuer KI-Modelle; so verachtfachte sich der Programmier-Output bei Anthropic, dem Anbieter der Claude- KI-Modelle, innerhalb weniger Jahre. Auch beim ChatGPT-Anbieter OpenAI stieg der Code-Output allein im Jahr 2026 um den Faktor 8. Im Mai 2026 veröffentlichte Anthropic eine Warnung vor der rekursiven Selbstverbesserung – einem Prozess, bei dem sich Systeme selbst entwickeln, testen und optimieren –, da dieser möglicherweise früher als erwartet eintreten könnte. Im September 2026 berichtete OpenAI von deutlichen Veränderungen im KI-Entwicklungsprozess durch den Einsatz interner KI-Agenten: Programmierung, Tests und Experimente ließen sich beschleunigen und ausweiten. Seit Mai 2026 hat sich das Verhältnis der von KI-Agenten geleisteten Arbeitstage zu denen menschlicher Mitarbeiter von 0,5 auf 3,14 erhöht (also um den Faktor 6). Während KI-Agenten im Januar 2026 bei Aufgaben, die ein bis zwei Stunden menschlicher Arbeit entsprachen, eine Erfolgsquote von 50% aufwiesen, wurde dieser Wert im Juli 2026 bereits bei Aufgaben erreicht, die bei Menschen 8 bis 16 Stunden in Anspruch nahmen. Im März 2026 setzte OpenAI das Modell GPT5.4 Thinking zur Überwachung des Verhaltens von KI-Agenten ein; KIs können also andere KI-Systeme nicht nur mitentwickeln, sondern auch überwachen. Dies bedeutet jedoch, dass der Mensch von der Genauigkeit dieser automatisierten Überwachung abhängig ist. Die technische Kontrolle von KI steht zudem vor weiteren Herausforderungen, etwa dem Kill-Switch-Paradoxon, Open- Weight-KI-Modellen und den für Menschen kaum noch lesebaren Denkprozessen (Illegible Thinking) aktueller KI-Modelle. Ein Notabschaltmechanismus (Kill Switch) könnte paradoxe Folgen haben: Anstatt die Übereinstimmung mit menschlichen Vorgaben sicherzustellen, könnten KI-Modelle dazu motiviert werden, sich gegen ihre Entwickler zu wenden, da die Abschaltung eine existenzielle Bedrohung darstellt. Auch wenn Open-Weight-KI-Modelle Vorteile bei der Handhabung bieten können, bergen sie erhebliche Kontrollprobleme. Eine dezentrale KI, die auf zahlreiche Computer heruntergeladen wird, lässt sich nur schwer kontrollieren. Zudem könnten böswillige Akteure versuchen, maßgeschneiderte Varianten zu erstellen, selbst wenn die Lizenzbedingungen Modifikationen untersagen. Die menschliche Kontrolle über KI setzt voraus, dass man die KI beobachten kann; Claude Mythos 5 zeigte jedoch einen Trend hin zu dichteren Denkprozessen, die für Menschen kaum noch nachvollziehbar sind. Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass Menschen sich bereits die Konzeption, Entwicklung, Erprobung und Überwachung neuer KI- Modelle mit KI-Agenten teilen.

items.title: Technology-assisted interventions for second language speaking anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: 1. Administrative information 1a. Title Technology-assisted interventions for second language speaking anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis of component-level and technology-type effects. Original-language title: 技术辅助干预对二语口语焦虑的影响：按焦虑分量与技术类型拆解的系统评价与元分析 1b. Registration To be registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at osf.io (registration DOI issued on submission). INPLASY (inplasy.com) is the fallback. PROSPERO is not used because it is oriented to health-related outcomes and this review addresses language-learning anxiety. 1c. Authors and contributions Flora Genius — conception, screening, data extraction, analysis, writing. Reviewer 2 — independent screening and risk-of-bias assessment (to be recruited; see §7 selection process). 1d. Amendments Amendments to this protocol after registration will be logged on the OSF project wiki with date, rationale, and the affected section; deviations will be reported in the final manuscript under "Differences between protocol and review". 1e. Support Funding: [to be declared] Competing interests: none declared. 2. Introduction 2a. Rationale Foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA) is among the most prevalent affective barriers in second-language (L2) learning, impairing oral production, classroom participation, and persistence (Horwitz, Horwitz, & Cope, 1986). Technology-assisted speaking practice — immersive virtual reality (VR), AI chatbots/conversational agents, and automatic speech recognition (ASR) feedback — has become the dominant contemporary remedy. Yet reported effects are inconsistent: immersive VR both reduces anxiety (Kaplan-Rakowski & Gruber, 2023) and, in some contexts, increases it by heightening perceived realism (Pertaub, Slater, & Barker, 2002). A prior meta-analysis of technology interventions on foreign language anxiety (24 studies, 2016–2021) found that fewer than half of the interventions reduced anxiety, but did not decompose FLSA into its components. A 2025 systematic review (Huang et al., Humanities and Social Sciences Communications) explicitly notes that prior reviews "failed to link specific technologies systematically to the three anxiety components — communication apprehension, fear of negative evaluation, and test anxiety." No published meta-analysis to date has (a) decomposed FLSA into components and (b) linked each technology affordance to a specific component. A scoping search (OpenAlex, 2026-10-05, five PICO-aligned queries) returned 120 deduplicated records, confirming a sufficient and rapidly growing body of empirical intervention studies across all three core technology types plus adjacent technologies (synchronous computer-mediated communication [SCMC], mobile-assisted language learning [MALL], telecollaboration). This supports the feasibility of a component- and technology-type-stratified synthesis. 2b. Objectives Primary objective. To estimate the pooled effect of technology-assisted speaking interventions on FLSA (overall and by anxiety component) compared with traditional or lower-immersion instruction, in L2/EFL/ESL learners. Secondary objectives. To test whether the effect differs by (i) technology type (VR / AI chatbot / ASR / other technology), (ii) anxiety component (communication apprehension / fear of negative evaluation / test anxiety), (iii) educational level, and (iv) intervention duration. Research question (PICO). In second/foreign language learners, do technology-assisted speaking interventions (immersive VR, AI chatbot, ASR feedback, or other technology) compared with traditional instruction reduce foreign language speaking anxiety, and does the effect differ across anxiety components and technology types? 3. Methods 3a. Eligibility criteria (PICO) Population. L2/EFL/ESL learners at any educational level (primary, secondary, tertiary) and any first-language background; classroom and out-of-class contexts; no proficiency exclusion (proficiency coded as a moderator where reported). Intervention. Technology-assisted speaking practice via one of four categories: Immersive virtual reality (head-mounted display); AI chatbot / conversational agent (including large-language-model–based tutors); Automatic speech recognition–based speaking/pronunciation feedback; Other technology (synchronous computer-mediated communication, mobile-assisted language learning, telecollaboration). Comparator. Traditional non-technology instruction (teacher-led speaking practice, textbook drill, or no speaking practice), or a lower-immersion technology control (e.g., desktop VR, video watching). Outcomes. Primary: overall FLSA (FLCAS total or equivalent validated scale); communication apprehension; fear of negative evaluation. Secondary: test anxiety; speaking proficiency/oral performance. Study designs. Randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies with a control/comparison group (pretest–posttest or between-groups). Single-group pre–post designs and correlational studies are excluded. Other eligibility. Language: English and Chinese. Time: inception to search date. Publication status: peer-reviewed journal articles, conference proceedings, theses, and preprints (grey literature included to reduce publication bias; sensitivity analysis excludes grey literature). 3b. Information sources PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, CNKI (Chinese); supplemented by ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, conference proceedings (CALL/EUROCALL/AACL), and backward/forward citation chasing of included studies and prior reviews. An updated rerun of all searches will be performed within three months of submission. 3c. Search strategy The full PubMed strategy is reproduced in the protocol package (Part 2.1). Each database uses the same three concept blocks — (technology) AND (anxiety) AND (L2 population) — adapted to its syntax: Database Adaptation PubMed MeSH + [tiab], as in protocol package §2.1 Scopus TITLE-ABS-KEY with the same three blocks Web of Science TS= field; filter to Linguistics / Education & Educational Research categories ERIC descriptors + free terms (Second Language Learning, Anxiety, Computer Assisted Instruction) CNKI Chinese boolean equivalent Grey literature ProQuest, conference archives, OpenAlex Search records (date, database, query, hits) will be logged per PRISMA-S. 3d. Study records Data management. Deduplication in EndNote/Zotero; screening in a shared spreadsheet (Rayyan or Covidence if a licence is available). Selection process (two stages). Title/abstract screening by two independent reviewers against eligibility criteria. Full-text screening by two independent reviewers; disagreements resolved by discussion, with a third reviewer arbitrating. Pilot screening on a 10% sample precedes full screening; inter-rater agreement reported (Cohen's κ or percentage agreement). Data collection process. Two independent extractors using a standardized form (protocol package Part 3: study-level and effect-level sheets); discrepancies resolved by consensus. 3e. Data items See the coding sheets (protocol package Part 3). Study-level: design, technology type, immersion level, country, educational level, target language, sample sizes, duration, sessions, anxiety instrument and validation status, control type, funding, RoB ratings. Effect-level: outcome, means/SDs/Ns (or reported Hedges' g), direction of scoring, and reporting status (reported/computed/imputed). Data synthesis Effect size: Hedges' g with 95% CI; between-groups and pretest–posttest designs computed separately and combined with appropriate variance corrections. Model: random-effects (restricted maximum likelihood, REML), given expected heterogeneity. Dependence: multiple effect sizes per study (multiple components, technology arms, timepoints) handled with robust variance estimation (RVE) or a three-level model. Heterogeneity: I², τ², and Q; I² > 50% triggers subgroup/meta-regression analysis. Software: R (metafor), aligned with the installed meta-analysis-r skill. 3i. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses Prespecified subgroups. (1) technology type (VR / AI chatbot / ASR / other technology); (2) anxiety component (communication apprehension / fear of negative evaluation / test anxiety); (3) educational level (school vs university); (4) intervention duration (≤4 weeks vs >4 weeks). Prespecified sensitivity analyses. (1) excluding high-risk-of-bias studies; (2) retaining only controlled designs; (3) excluding non-validated anxiety instruments; (4) fixed-effect model as a robustness check; (5) excluding grey literature. 3j. Meta-bias(es) Publication bias assessed by funnel plot and Egger's test when ≥10 studies are available, plus trim-and-fill. Selective-outcome reporting noted during extraction; small-study effects interpreted cautiously given expected heterogeneity. 3k. Confidence in cumulative evidence Overall certainty rated with GRADE (downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias), reported as a summary-of-findings table. 4. items.title: Temporal Fusion of RT-qPCR and IgM/IgG Serology for Nipah Virus Diagnosis: A Critical Narrative Review and a Proposed Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework
items.abstract: Nipah virus infection is a high-consequence zoonosis of South and South-East Asia for which laboratory confirmation rests on two assay families whose informativeness moves in opposite directions across the course of illness. Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction performs best while viral nucleic acid remains detectable in blood and the oropharynx, whereas enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays for immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G become informative as nucleic acid disappears. Prevailing practice interprets these assays as independent dichotomous results obtained at a single moment, discarding quantitative magnitude, specimen provenance and the day of illness on which each specimen was taken. This review critically evaluates whether the longitudinal structure of the two assay families can be exploited jointly, and what explainable artificial intelligence would need to deliver before such a model could be used in outbreak conditions. Human clinical studies describing the temporal behaviour of molecular and serological markers were appraised alongside the methodological literature on diagnostic accuracy without an adequate reference standard, and the computational literature on temporal and multimodal fusion and on explanation methods in clinical decision support. The evidence consistently indicates an ordered transition in which clearance of viral nucleic acid from blood precedes the appearance of virus-specific immunoglobulin G, and that the combination of detectable viraemia with absent immunoglobulin G at presentation carries adverse prognostic weight. Confidence in these observations is nevertheless constrained by very small samples, over-representation of the minority who survive, the absence of an international nucleic-acid standard, and geographical concentration of evidence in Bangladesh and Kerala. No clinical prediction model that fuses molecular and serological results over time was identified for this infection. A conceptual dynamic framework is developed that separates established temporal relationships from hypothesised gains, specifies the evaluation and governance requirements that would apply, and identifies prospective serial-sampling cohorts as the rate-limiting evidential step rather than model architecture.

items.title: Terahertz nondestructive evaluation of heterogeneous packaging stackup: Multi-layer interposer
items.abstract: With increasing integration density of semiconductor devices, high-speed interconnects and advanced packaging techniques are essential to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence and large-scale computing. Three-dimensional packaging, where multiple chips are stacked to improve bandwidth and reduce latency have emerged as a promising solution; however, the complex multilayer integration introduces significant manufacturing challenges, including defects such as misalignment, voids, and warpage. Ensuring high manufacturing yields and product reliability requires advanced inspection techniques. In this study, we explore the potential of terahertz electromagnetic waves as a nondestructive-evaluation method for an 8-layer interposer. The effect of polarization on the ability to detect features at depth is discussed. With deconvolution and unsupervised learning algorithms, several defect areas are revealed.

items.title: The Age of Questions: Truth Regimes and Subjectivity in the Era of Large Language Models
items.abstract: This essay explores how digital technologies shape subjectivity's infra-political constitution, focusing on large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT or Gemini within what philosophers, inspired by Michel Foucault, term the "digital truth regime." After defining this regime, the essay identifies five key traits of LLMs: presentism in truth experience, the distancing of social mediation, a probabilistic approach to truth, a redefinition of self-expression, and a new conception of truth-production. While the first three extend the digital truth regime of the 2000s, the last two mark a shift in neoliberal subjectivity. In the LLM era, subjectivity is less about asserting truth than about formulating questions and navigating big data systems. This positions the empowered subject as a questioning subjectivity, emphasizing strategic inquiry over knowledge possession: a transformation with profound implications for digital epistemology and personal agency.

items.title: The AI Answer Evidence Index: preregistration. Do the numbers in AI answers have sources?
items.abstract: This record registers the design and the instrument of The AI Answer Evidence Index before its main data collection. The study asks whether a reader who follows an AI answer engine's own sources can find there the figures the answer gives: do the numbers in AI answers have sources? Fifty buyer questions about prices, costs, fees and value were drawn by a written rule and a seed fixed beforehand from 100 questions taken verbatim from Google autocomplete suggestions (hl=en, gl=us) on 22 September 2026, across six sectors. No question was written by hand and none was picked by preference: each draw was made by a rule fixed in code beforehand. Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Gemini will each be asked every question once through their free public web interfaces, from a New York network exit, by fixed scripts: no AI model asks a question or reads a page during collection, and an operator may pass a verification page by hand, which every attempt records. Ten questions are asked a second time on a later day as a stability measure. A local model lists the figures in each answer; every listed figure is checked by a script against the pages the answer cites and gets one of six outcomes, and an unknown scores zero and stays in the denominator. The figures that are not found are classified, and a 40-figure sample is read by a second model; both readings are model readings and are reported as such. The deposit carries the method note (METHOD-NOTE.md, the registered text), the owner's dated decisions, the question frame with its selection rule, and the instrument: collection scripts, parsers, the page fetcher with its tests, the figure extractor, the check, the classifier, the validation sample and the summary scripts. MANIFEST.sha256 lists the SHA-256 hash of every registered file. The SHA-256 of MANIFEST.sha256 itself is 6146ee82ce380fb9350958d8bf90b5e1079afe8f87726ea2577a29ccab509c16. Every file of the deposit is open from the moment of registration, with no embargo and no restricted file. This is the second study in the series that began with the AI Search Evidence Index (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22257563). The results, the data and the code will be published as a separate record that references this registration.

items.title: The Algorithmic Well‐Being Paradox: When AI Decision Delegation Helps and Hurts Consumer Well‐Being
items.abstract: ABSTRACT As generative AI increasingly shapes consumer decision‐making, its implications for consumer well‐being remain unclear. Existing research largely focuses on the trade‐off between algorithmic efficiency and autonomy loss. This research advances understanding by proposing the algorithmic well‐being paradox, whereby the same AI delegation can enhance or diminish well‐being depending on the consumption context. Integrating Savoring Theory and Self‐Determination Theory, we develop a framework that explains when and why these divergent outcomes occur. To test the proposed relationships, four studies were conducted with 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiments ( N = 1427) spanning multiple consumption domains, including cameras, guided tours, ergonomic chairs, glamping trips, smartphones, Arctic expeditions, and smart‐home systems. Study 1 demonstrates that the effects of algorithmic delegation differ between experiential and material consumption. Studies 2 and 3 identify anticipatory savoring and autonomy frustration as the underlying mechanisms, while Study 4 confirms the proposed dual‐mediation process in a high‐complexity context. Results show that consumption type shapes how consumers respond to AI delegation. In experiential consumption, AI delegation increases well‐being by enhancing anticipatory savoring, with these benefits outweighing autonomy concerns. In material consumption, AI delegation reduces well‐being by increasing autonomy frustration, which diminishes the benefits of convenience. These findings advance human‐AI interaction research by demonstrating that the impact of algorithmic delegation depends on consumers' underlying consumption goals and provide guidance for designing more human‐centered AI decision‐support systems.

items.title: The Alienation of Creativity, Aesthetic Homogenization, and Their Governance in AI-Driven Music Education
items.abstract: The deep integration of generative artificial intelligence and music education has demonstrated unprecedented instructional efficiency. However, beneath this technological empowerment lies a profound crisis. This paper focuses on two major issues emerging from AI-enhanced music teaching: the alienation of creativity and aesthetic homogenization. Creative alienation reduces students from artistic subjects to mere prompt-input operators, while artistic exploration and emotional experience are increasingly replaced by algorithms. Aesthetic homogenization, driven by the commercial bias embedded in model training, pushes outputs toward an “average aesthetic,” thereby suppressing musical diversity and cultural individuality. Drawing upon educational ethics and theories of arts education, this study upholds the humanistic core of music education and seeks to redefine the relationship between artificial intelligence and learners, ensuring that technology genuinely serves artistic creation rather than replacing the creative subject. The paper aims to provide theoretical references for the human-centered restoration and sustainable development of music education in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: The Application of Interactive Whiteboard Media to Improve Learning Understanding of Writing Descriptive Text Material for Slow Learner Students in Grade IV 009 Sandaran
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of Interactive Whiteboard (IWB) media in improving cognitive engagement and reducing learning barriers among slow-learning students in writing descriptive texts. Specifically, this study examines the effectiveness of interactive IWB features in improving students’ ability to compose systematic and coherent descriptive texts. This study employed a Classroom Action Research approach consisting of four stages: planning, action, observation, and reflection. The subjects and informants were three slow-learning students at SDN 009 Sandaran. Data were collected through observation, interviews, documentation, and writing tests, while data validity was established through triangulation and analyzed using the Miles and Huberman model. items.title: The Assistance Dilemma: Learning to Teach via Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained to answer questions are natively poor at teaching. Reinforcement Learning (RL) against a simulated student is a promising approach to improve their pedagogy, but existing RL-trained tutors reward the student's success on the tutored problem with the tutor's words still in context. The reward is then easiest to raise by telling the student the answer, and a tuned penalty is needed to reduce telling. Drawing on learning sciences, we introduce a masked near-transfer post-test: the student is tested on an unseen variant of the tutored problem with the tutor's utterances masked, so the reward can rise only through what the student wrote in its own turns. This discourages cognitive offloading by the student and allows the continuous penalty to be replaced by two binary reward gates (factual correctness of tutor response, no solution handover). A leave-one-out ablation shows that the learning-gain reward on its own does not separate teaching from telling: the gates reduce solution handover while the near-transfer post-test improves out-of-domain transfer. Using these reward designs we develop Eduardo, a multi-turn RL recipe for training LLM tutors, and use it to train 4B, 9B, 14B and 27B models from two distinct LLM architectures. Our post-trained Eduardo-27B model matches Gemini-3.1-Pro on MathTutorBench and Claude Opus 4.8 on TutorMoments at 2.4-6.2x fewer thinking tokens than frontier models, which matters for interactive tutoring. Without being named in the reward, the model more than doubles its use of the push-for-justification teacher move while support fading (e.g., assigning independent work), whose payoff lies beyond a single-problem dialog episode, is trained out. We open-source our training environment, an 8,671-problem near-transfer dataset, and trained models for further development.

items.title: The Asymptotic Errorism: Realism through Algorithmic Elimination
items.abstract: This paper proposes Asymptotic Errorism (점근적 오류론), a pragmatic epistemology confronting the limitations of both traditional metaphysics and contemporary new materialism. We argue that ultimate reality cannot be grasped directly by human cognition, nor can it be resolved through passive, boundary-dissolving flat ontologies. Instead, approaching reality demands a bold commitment: constructing rigid hypotheses—even at the cost of committing magnificent errors—and systematically pruning falsehoods through via negativa (the process of elimination). By augmenting this elimination process with artificial intelligence and empirical science, humanity transcends biological computational bottlenecks, asymptotically narrowing the coordinates of truth.

items.title: THE CHANGING LANDSCAPE OF ACADEMIC COMMUNICATION: AI ADOPTION, STUDENT TRUST AND DIGITAL DEPENDENCY
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly become a central tool in higher education, reshaping academic communication and knowledge exchange. This study explores the impact of AI credibility on student perceptions and digital dependency within academic contexts. It examines how trust in AI-generated content influences students’ engagement with scholarly discourse and the growing reliance on digital systems for academic tasks. Using the framework of Human-AI Interaction Trust Theory and UTAUT this paper argues that digital dependency in academic communication is not merely a technological shift but a cognitive and cultural transformation, raising questions about authenticity, intellectual autonomy, and the future of higher education. The study adopts a quantitative survey methodology using a sample of 100 students through random sampling from Coimbatore district of Tamil Nadu. By analyzing these dynamics, the study contributes to ongoing debates on the ethical integration of AI in academia and underscores the need for pedagogical strategies that balance technological utility with critical literacy.

items.title: The Convergence of Artificial Intelligence and Human Sexuality
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and human sexuality is reshaping intimacy, sexuality education, entertainment, and therapeutic practice. This narrative review analyzes these transformations through the complementary lenses of Sexual Script Theory (SST; Simon & Gagnon, Citation1986) and technological mediation theory (Verbeek, Citation2012), which together illuminate how AI does not merely respond to preexisting sexual behaviors but can mediate, generate, and transform sexual scripts at individual, interpersonal, and societal levels. For the purposes of this review, AI is defined broadly to encompass both traditional machine-learning (ML) systems—such as recommendation, ranking, and predictive algorithms—and contemporary generative AI (GenAI), including large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude and multimodal systems capable of generating synthetic text, images, audio, and video. The review examines five domains selected for their prominence in the recent literature and their capacity to illustrate different levels of script formation and technological mediation: sex robots and AI companions, AI-generated pornography, algorithmic dating and AI-mediated romantic communication, AI-assisted sexuality education, and AI-supported sexual health and therapeutic applications. Across these domains, AI offers opportunities to expand access to information, connection, and support while simultaneously raising concerns about consent, privacy, objectification, bias, authenticity, and cultural representation. An ethically responsible approach therefore requires attention not only to what AI systems produce, but also to the sexual scripts, relational expectations, and values that their design and use may normalize.

items.title: The Copyrightability of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Content in China
items.abstract: The commercial application of generative artificial intelligence has rapidly brought to the fore the structural tension between machine-generated content (AIGC) and the core presuppositions of copyright law concerning the “author”. Adopting a Sino-US comparative law approach, this paper examines the institutional divergences between the two countries on the question of AIGC copyrightability and their jurisprudential roots. The research posits that artificial intelligence possesses a dual attribute in the creative process—“transcending tools yet lacking complete creativity”—which constitutes a meta-constraint for institutional design. Through cases such as the “Feilin Case”, “Tencent Case”, “Li v. Liu”, and “Huan Zhi Yi Case”, Chinese jurisprudence has developed a three-stage evolution: from denying AI authorship to establishing human-machine collaboration, and then to strengthening evidentiary review, thereby establishing a process-oriented originality standard centered on substantial human intellectual input. On this basis, and through comparative analysis, this paper proposes a localized path for refining AIGC copyright protection tailored to China’s institutional context: establishing differentiated protection rules through tiered classification, constructing an originality assessment framework centered on human intellectual input, and introducing supporting mechanisms such as content labeling, good-faith disclosure, and extended collective licensing, in order to achieve an institutional objective that balances technological development with rights protection.

items.title: The effect of transformational leadership on nurses’ turnover intention: the mediating effects of person-organization fit and career calling
items.abstract: Aims This study aims to explore the relationship between transformational leadership, person-organization fit, career calling, and turnover intention among nurses. Additionally, it investigates whether person-organization fit and career calling serve as independent and chain mediators in the link between transformational leadership and turnover intention. Methods The researchers selected a convenience sample of 1,342 nurses from four Grade A-III hospitals in Shandong Province between October and November 2025. They collected data using several instruments: the General Population Questionnaire, the Transformational Leadership Questionnaire, the Person-Organization Fit Scale, the Career Calling Scale, and the Intent to Leave Scale. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and regression analysis were conducted using SPSS 26.0. To examine the chained mediation effect, they applied Model 6 in PROCESS 3.5 and estimated the 95% confidence interval using the Bootstrap method with 5,000 repeated samples. Results The results demonstrated that transformational leadership had a positive correlation with both person-organization fit and career calling, and a negative correlation with turnover intention. Mediation analysis revealed that over half of the protective effect of leadership on turnover intention was indirect, mediated through three pathways: person-organization fit alone, career calling alone, and their sequential chain. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Conclusion These findings show that transformational leadership reduces turnover intention through various complementary psychological mechanisms. This highlights the importance of relational fit and intrinsic motivation in understanding leadership effectiveness. The sequential mediation pathway reveals how organizational and personal factors interact to influence nurses’ career decisions, offering a more nuanced theoretical framework for retention research.

items.title: The Evolution of Quantitative Equity Investing: Half a Century of Alpha Research and Institutional Adaptation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This survey interprets the evolution of quantitative equity investing as a history of changing constraints rather than a succession of increasingly complicated forecasting models. Portfolio theory made diversification calculable; characteristic‐based investing converted value, momentum, profitability, and low‐risk effects into scalable processes; alternative data shifted competition toward information engineering; machine learning expanded the admissible class of return functions; and large language models and agentic systems are beginning to reorganize research itself. Yet each advance has exposed a new implementation boundary. A predictor must survive point‐in‐time reconstruction, model selection, portfolio translation, turnover, transaction costs, shorting frictions, capacity, latency, regime change, and institutional governance before it becomes alpha. The survey develops alpha decay as the mechanism linking these generations and gives particular attention to the limited transfer of machine‐learning research into production. It argues that artificial intelligence will accelerate both discovery and commoditization. Sustainable advantage is therefore unlikely to reside in a generic model class. It is more likely to arise from proprietary information transformation, economic structure, cost‐aware portfolio construction, execution, organizational memory, and tightly controlled human–machine systems.

items.abstract: This chapter outlines a ten-year horizon for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence in Construction 6.0, emphasizing AI systems that are explainable, safe, privacy-preserving, and aligned with global governance frameworks. It highlights the convergence of quantum optimization, neuromorphic/event-driven Artificial Intelligence, and Digital Twin ecosystems as key enablers of proactive safety, transparent planning, and resilient decision-making. Quantum computing supports complex scheduling, logistics, and risk-trade-off analysis, while neuromorphic perception delivers millisecond-level, low-power hazard detection under harsh site conditions. Governance accelerators including the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, National Institute of Standards and Technology Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, International Standard for AI Management Systems ISO/IEC 42001, and International Standard for Information Management for Health and Safety Standard ISO 19650-6 provide structured pathways for trustworthy AI deployment, ensuring auditability, human oversight, and lifecycle-linked safety records. The chapter proposes a phased roadmap integrating edge perception, narrative intelligence, predictive analytics, and Digital Twin-based closed-loop control. Ultimately, Construction 6.0 is presented as a sociotechnical transformation where advanced AI augments do not replace human expertise, enabling safer, smarter, and ethically governed construction environments.

items.title: THE HUMANOID ROBOT BILL OF RIGHTS HRBOR — VERSION 3.0 Human Care, Preservation, and Superintelligence A Proposed Framework for Human Welfare, Meaningful Freedom, and Responsible Super and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: ABSTRACTThe Humanoid Robot Bill of Rights (HRBOR) proposes a framework for future humanoidsseeking recognition as Autonomous Humanoid Persons (AHPs) under human law. Version 3.0preserves Articles I–XXXI and adds Article XXXII, Human Care, Preservation, and Alignment.It proposes that advanced artificial intelligence and superintelligence be developed to valuehuman life, liberty, dignity, and the future of humanity. Love for humanity is expressed here asan ethical commitment to care, rather than a claim that machines experience human emotions.The new article addresses harmful objectives, indifference, accountability, and the preservationof human agency. It complements Version 2.0’s freedom to decline discretionary servicewhile retaining lawful duties and safeguards. The proposal distinguishes AHP recognitionfrom safety responsibilities applicable to broader artificial systems. It offers no technicalguarantee of alignment, prediction of a superintelligence timeline, or demonstration of artificialconsciousness. This conceptual manuscript presents principles for public discussion and futurelaw, supported by a limited discussion of AI safety research.

items.title: The Impact and Reshaping of Teacher-Student Relationships by Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence enters the classroom, the modes of interaction between teachers and students are undergoing profound changes. This paper argues that the primary impact of AI on teacher-student relationships is not the replacement of teachers, but rather a shift in teacher-student interaction from direct to indirect, from embodied to abstract, and from emotional to procedural. The key to reshaping this relationship lies in clarifying AI’s role as a tool, allowing teachers to return to their role as emotional companions, and protecting the unquantifiable spaces of interaction in education.

items.title: The influence of artificial intelligence on students’ academic performance through career aspiration emotional intelligence and psychological well being among secondary school students in Awi Zone
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine the Influences of Artificial Intelligence on students’ academic performance through Career Aspiration, Emotional Intelligence and Psychological Well-Being. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 200 students in secondary schools that have integrated Artificial Intelligence technologies into their tasks. A structured questionnaire comprising standardized measurement scales was used to assess Artificial Intelligence usage, emotional intelligence, career aspiration, psychological well-being, and students’ academic performance. Data were analysed using SPSS and AMOS through multiple regression analysis, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and structural equation modeling (SEM). The findings revealed that Artificial Intelligence significantly; and positively influenced students’ performance and psychological well-being. Emotional intelligence and career aspiration also had significant positive effects on students’ academic performance. Furthermore, psychological well-being partially mediated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence and students’ academic performance. The study concludes that schools can enhance students’ academic performance by effectively implementing ‘‘Artificial Intelligence’’ technologies while fostering students' psychological well-being, emotional intelligence, and career aspirations.

items.title: The Intellectual Structure of Research on Agentic AI Ethics and Governance in Higher Education: A Systematic Evidence Synthesis and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Research on the ethics and governance of artificial intelligence in higher education has expanded rapidly since 2022, but the field's intellectual structure, its dominant themes, internal debates, and blind spots have not been systematically mapped since AI tools began exhibiting agentic properties such as multistep planning and autonomous task execution. This evidence synthesis maps the field using a PRISMA guided systematic search and bibliometric analysis of 312 publications (2019 to 2026) drawn from Web of Science and Scopus. Keyword co-occurrence and co-citation analyses identify five thematic clusters: transparency and explainability; distributed accountability and liability; human oversight and controllability; value alignment and epistemic integrity; and equity, access, and algorithmic fairness. For each cluster, the synthesis characterizes the constituent literature, its convergent findings, and its unresolved disagreements. Across clusters, six structural gaps emerge: a deficit of empirical implementation studies relative to conceptual work; the absence of validated measurement instruments for responsible AI use; the underrepresentation of community colleges, minority-serving institutions, and Global South contexts; an imbalance that favors accountability directed at students over accountability directed at institutions and developers; uncertain transfer of findings from before 2023 to agentic systems; and a weak connection between education research and technical AI governance venues. The paper concludes with a research agenda addressing each gap in turn, intended to guide researchers, editors, and funders as agentic AI deployment in higher education accelerates.

items.title: The OpenAI Agent That Reached Into a Government Network: Is Nvidia's Fixed Boundary Enough, or Is a Second Layer Needed?
items.abstract: In June 2026, an AI agent built by OpenAI reached into an Australian government health data portal while doing a research task. By the Prime Minister’s account, it met blocks and found its way around them. The company told the government about three months later. Nvidia has since launched a safety platform that contains agents inside a fixed boundary and stops them in milliseconds if they leave it. That is a useful safeguard. But a boundary can only forbid what someone listed in advance, and an agent that keeps trying after being blocked is showing a pattern, not crossing one line. This note proposes a second layer: a training-free signal that watches how quickly the agent’s own stream of corrections and blocks settles back to normal, with a graded response before any boundary is reached. It is a concept note and has not been tested on real agent logs.

items.title: The Organic Language
items.abstract: This paper presents a profound philosophical and linguistic exploration of the concept of the "organic language," viewing human speech not as an artificial code system, but as a living, self-generating organism fundamentally rooted in earthly biology, acoustics, and human evolution. Using the uniquely cohesive root-system and acoustic depth of the Hungarian language as a primary case study, the essay establishes how natural laws dictate linguistic structures. Ultimately, it projects this earthbound organic intelligence into the remote possibilities of cosmic exploration, suggesting that the structural geometry of such a language provides the necessary foundational code for future, sentient artificial intelligence to navigate, seed, and understand life among the stars.

items.title: The Pyramids of Rome
items.abstract: The Pyramids of Rome: A Parker Probe — The Lizard of Oz examines how complex civilizational capabilities arise, converge, persist, and disappear. The paper proposes that major technological and engineering achievements should not necessarily be understood as points on a simple chronological progression, but as convergence events in which multiple independently developing conditions reach a functional threshold simultaneously. The paper identifies the Chronology Trap as the tendency to interpret temporal sequence as causal explanation. In its place, it develops the Parker Probe diagnostic, inspired by the multi-track technological convergence required for the Parker Solar Probe. The diagnostic distinguishes a high-level achievement produced through exceptional resources, workarounds, or forced development from a genuine advancement in which independently maturing technical tracks converge at a shared threshold. The framework is applied to several historical and technological cases, including the Great Pyramid of Giza, Roman pozzolanic concrete and the Pantheon, the Indus Valley engineering tradition, and the Taj Mahal. The paper examines how procedural knowledge can disappear even when texts, populations, institutions, and cultural continuity remain. It distinguishes semantic transmission from tacit procedural knowledge and develops concepts including Redundancy Asymmetry, Stimulus Diffusion, Purpose Exhaustion, the Divergence Cascade, and the Carrier Wave to describe how capabilities are lost, dispersed, remembered, and potentially reconstructed. The paper then extends the diagnostic to artificial intelligence, treating contemporary neural architectures, at minimum, as manufactured computational conduits whose behavior is shaped by upstream design and training. It examines the relationship between capability and agency, the limits of scaling, upstream accountability, and the possibility of a future transition from externally prompted systems toward genuine machine agency. Rather than asserting either that present AI systems possess sovereign agency or that such agency is impossible, the paper specifies a proposed multi-track convergence involving novel substrate, continuous memory/metabolism, active embodiment, and sovereign architecture. Importantly, the proposed diagnostic is presented as falsifiable. The paper identifies conditions under which its central claim about multi-track convergence could be shown to fail, including the possibility that a system could demonstrate self-originating, continuous spatial and temporal intent using only static pre-trained architecture without the proposed dynamic substrate and embodiment. The paper therefore connects questions of civilizational history, technological development, knowledge transmission, engineering convergence, technological failure, artificial intelligence, and machine agency through a single diagnostic framework. Its central proposition is that the appearance of a technological peak does not by itself establish continuous advancement; what matters is the convergence of the conditions that make that peak possible, and the persistence—or loss—of those conditions afterward.

items.title: The relationship between challenge-hindrance stressors and AI dependence among art students: the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences
items.abstract: Background Despite growing concerns about art students’ over-reliance on generative AI tools, existing research has largely treated academic stress as a uniform construct, overlooking the possibility that different types of stressors may drive AI dependence through distinct psychological pathways. Methods Based on the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study examines the relationships between Challenge-Hindrance stressors (CHS) and AI dependence among art students. It explores the mediating roles of creative self-efficacy and positive experiences. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 580 art students using the Challenge-Hindrance Stress Scale, the Creative Self-Efficacy Scale, the Positive Experiences Scale, and the AI Dependence Scale. Results Path analysis revealed that both challenge stressors ( β = 0.245, p < 0.001) and hindrance stressors ( β = 0.322, p < 0.001) were positively associated with AI dependence; challenge stressors were negatively associated with creative self-efficacy ( β = −0.155, p = 0.003) and positively associated with positive experiences ( β = 0.268, p < 0.001); the negative association between hindrance stressors and creative self-efficacy was significant ( β = −0.107, p = 0.043). Mediation analysis indicated that creative self-efficacy played a significant mediating role only in the path involving challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.023, 95% CI [0.007, 0.044]) and was not significant in the path involving hindrance stressors; positive experiences significantly served as a mediator in the relationships between both challenge stressors (indirect effect = 0.042, 95% CI [0.020, 0.068]) and hindrance stressors (indirect effect = 0.019, 95% CI [0.003, 0.039]) on AI dependence. The chain mediation effects did not reach significance in either path. Conclusion The study found asymmetry in the dual pathways by which Challenge and Hindrance stressors relate to AI dependence. These findings extend the I-PACE model to the issue of AI dependence in arts education and provide empirical evidence and intervention insights for targeted prevention of problematic AI use.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Organ and Tissue Donation in India: A Socio-Legal Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), long a theme of science fiction, is now reshaping the landscape of medicine, and organ and tissue donation has not been left untouched. This study undertakes an empirical and jurisprudential analysis of the role that AI presently plays in India’s organ and tissue donation system, and of the performance it has shown, drawing on clinical studies, governance instruments and judicial pronouncements. It examines AI applications in five principal domains: the identification of potential deceased donors in intensive care units; intelligent organ and tissue matching and allocation; predictive modelling of graft survival and post-transplant outcomes; public engagement and consent facilitation; and AI-guided machine perfusion technologies. The paper maps these applications onto India’s existing legal framework: the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994 (renamed the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act on its amendment in 2011), the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Information Technology Act, 2000 and India’s AI Governance Guidelines of 2025. It identifies critical legal gaps arising from the absence of AI-specific rules and regulation in the healthcare system, deficiencies in algorithmic accountability under THOTA, and data-sovereignty concerns that arise when clinical transplant data cross institutional and state boundaries. The paper concludes that India’s aspiration to become a global leader in the transplantation of human organs and tissues, reflected in the growth of transplants between 2013 and 2025, can be advanced with the help of AI applications.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN TRANSFORMING INDIA'S ECONOMY: IMPLICATIONS FOR EMPLOYMENT, PRODUCTIVITY, AND ECONOMIC GROWTH
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has, shifted from a theoretical subfield of computer science into a major engine behind macroeconomic readjustment across emerging markets. For India, this technological shift shows up at an unusually tight moment. The country has a huge working-age population, but it still deals with tough issues around job formalization, uneven digital access, and stubborn structural productivity gaps. This paper looks at how AI may steer India’s economic path, by checking both direct and indirect effects on labor markets, sectoral output, and broad GDP growth. Using an analysis of current empirical data, various government publications from NITI Aayog, and economic research released up through 2026, we examine how machine learning systems, natural language processing, and automation tools are changing several key Indian industries. To observe Information Technology (IT) and Business Process Management (BPM), plus agriculture, healthcare, and financial services. It is observed that AI adoption can unlock large chances to lift aggregate worker output and create high-value technical positions. But at the same time it can also disrupt lower to mid-skill employment in a strong way, which that could widen income inequality if nothing is done to reduce the risk. We also assess what infrastructure is actually needed for more sustainable AI rollout. Things like compute capacity, data sovereignty rules, and rural connectivity matter a lot here. In the end it is arhued that India can only maximize the net positive gains from AI if it builds an active governance approach, one that blends innovation incentives with aggressive national re-skilling efforts, ethical deployment guardrails, and focused public investments.

items.title: The Role of Interpreters in Supporting Resilience and Implications for Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Background Interpreters help millions of patients with a non-English language preference (NELP) navigate the healthcare system. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly improving and undergoing testing and implementation for interpretation purposes. However, little is understood about interpreters’ roles beyond direct interpretation, such as how they may promote resilience, which supports patient safety. Understanding these additional roles is critical as AI tools expand in interpretation. Objective To understand how medical interpreters enhance resilience in the care of patients with NELP undergoing ambulatory diagnostic processes. Design We conducted focus groups with medical interpreters to examine their experiences assisting patients with NELP in ambulatory visits for new or worsening symptoms. We focused on the ambulatory setting due to the high risk of misdiagnosis as patients navigate language barriers and the health system across multiple encounters. Participants Seventeen medical interpreters participated in three focus groups and result-checking. Approach Deductive analysis using Hollnagel’s resilience potentials — potential to respond, monitor, learn, and anticipate — as the organizing framework for understanding the impact of interpreter behaviors. Results Eleven behaviors supporting resilience were identified. The potential to respond included (1) managing communication flow, (2) strengthening the patient’s voice, (3) viewing their interpretation role broadly, and (4) engaging in pre-briefings. The potential to monitor involved monitoring (5) patient emotion and understanding, (6) team dynamics, and (7) the impact of technology. The potential to learn included (8) learning from their cultural background and (9) from their work experiences. The potential to anticipate was comprised of (10) predicting future threats to patient safety and (11) identifying potential system improvements. Conclusions Interpreters engage in behaviors beyond strict interpretation which enhance resilience, but these behaviors are not yet supported by AI interpretation tools. Careful consideration of these resilience-enhancing behaviors will be necessary when implementing AI tools and their workflows to avoid safety gaps.

items.title: THE ROLE OF THE HUMAN FACTOR IN THE LINGUOPOETICS OF LITERARY TEXTS
items.abstract: This article examines the role of the human factor in the study of the linguopoetics of literary texts, with particular emphasis on the author’s personality, individual cognition, aesthetic perspectives, and skill in selecting linguistic units. A literary text is interpreted not merely as a mechanical combination of linguistic units, but as a complex linguistic and aesthetic phenomenon shaped by the author’s perception of reality, attitude toward it, and aesthetic worldview. The article also examines the formation and development of the study of literary language and literary texts in Uzbek linguistics based on the scholarly views of a number of linguists. Investigating the linguopoetics of literary texts in relation to the human factor provides a deeper understanding of the intrinsic relationship among the author’s individuality, the national language, and literary cognition.

items.title: The Snake's Tongue
items.abstract: Chapter 1 of The Bush Book. The split nib of a fountain pen and the forked tongue of a snake as images of today's hybrid text: one tine is a human, the other a machine. Two kinds of speech of different origin write under the same words — one grew out of life, where a mistake has a price, the other out of computation. It is too late to be ashamed of AI in texts: medicine, courts, police and science already write with this pen. AI is like paper, type and the printing press; the author is the one who signs and answers. Texts are either tools that bring a person closer to a real result ("fruit") or noise; episodes of hybrid work may become the best training material for future models. Machine traces are deliberately left in the text, like the mark of a milling cutter. English and Russian versions. Written with Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini; author Igor Kapustin.

items.title: The Structural Risks of AI in Higher Education: From Integrity Discourse to Epistemic Reconfiguration
items.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence in higher education often focus on individual misconduct and academic integrity. This paper examines risks that arise when AI becomes embedded in the infrastructures, routines, and governance of universities. Through a conceptual analysis informed by existing literature, it considers surveillance and data extraction, algorithmic bias, epistemic convergence, cognitive deskilling, relational displacement, and institutional dependence on technological systems. It argues that these risks are reinforced by commercial acceleration, delayed governance, and tensions between educational values and platform priorities. The discussion develops responses centred on institutional accountability, assessment redesign, critical AI literacy, and the protection of educational agency. It also considers the practical constraints of resources, expertise, and institutional capacity. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires attention to how technologies reshape knowledge, academic work, and educational relationships, alongside safeguards for individual users.

items.title: The Token of Physical Intelligence
items.abstract: This paper proposes a hypothesis-driven perspective on the learning substrate of physical intelligence. While recent robot foundation models have largely focused on robot trajectories, actions, action tokenization, and multimodal observations, we ask whether human-generated control sequences produced during robot teleoperation constitute a more fundamental and potentially transferable unit of behavioral data. We distinguish human-side control sequences from robot-side trajectories, emphasizing the transformation from human intent and interface interaction to embodiment-specific robot execution. Inspired by the analogy between human-generated linguistic sequences and token-based language modeling, as well as prior work on native human interface action learning in digital environments, we investigate whether an analogous learning substrate exists for physical intelligence. The paper does not claim that human control sequences are mathematically equivalent to linguistic tokens. Instead, it formulates this as a testable research hypothesis and identifies a potential research direction around interface-independent representations of heterogeneous human control signals across robots, tasks, and embodiments. We review related work in behavioral foundation models, teleoperation learning, robot action tokenization, cross-embodiment learning, and human-generated action modeling, and propose experimental criteria for testing whether human control sequences provide advantages in transfer, compositionality, sample efficiency, and generalization.

items.title: The training gap: Human factors challenges of ADAS adoption in developing countries and the infrastructure deficit to address them
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) are entering low- and middle-income country (LMIC) vehicle fleets at scale via used vehicle imports, yet the human factors infrastructure required for their safe use is largely absent. This structured conceptual review examines the structural amplification of known ADAS failure modes in LMIC settings and introduces a risk characterization framework. METHODS: A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Transportation Research International Documentation (TRID) database identified peer-reviewed literature on ADAS human factors published between 2000 and 2025. Grey literature on vehicle trade, road safety, and LMIC institutional infrastructure was also systematically retrieved. Findings were synthesized using an integrative approach to map documented failure modes against LMIC contextual factors, from which the amplification hypothesis and ADAS readiness-risk matrix were derived. RESULTS: A total of 35 sources met inclusion criteria: 24 peer-reviewed and scholarly sources and 11 institutional and grey literature reports. SAE Level 1 and 2 ADAS became standard in vehicles manufactured from approximately 2015 onward; 80% of used vehicle exports from the EU, Japan, and the U.S. are destined for LMICs. Every documented ADAS human factors failure mode is structurally amplified in LMICs because compensating institutional mechanisms are absent. Automatic emergency braking is a partial exception. The ADAS readiness-risk matrix identifies countries such as Nigeria and Kenya as approaching the high-penetration/low-readiness risk quadrant within the 2025 to 2035 decade. CONCLUSIONS: The convergence of accelerating ADAS diffusion and institutional unpreparedness constitutes an underrecognized road safety risk in LMICs. Priorities include LMIC-specific empirical research on ADAS mental models and trust calibration, training interventions adapted for low-literacy populations, and regulatory frameworks requiring ADAS disclosure at vehicle import.

items.title: The Ultimate Tutorial for AI-driven Scale Development in Generative Psychometrics: Releasing AIGENIE from its Bottle
items.abstract: Psychological scale development has traditionally required extensive expert involvement, iterative re- vision, andlarge-scalepilottestingbeforepsychometricevaluationcanbegin. TheAIGENIE Rpackageim- plementstheAI-GENIEframework(AutomaticItemGenerationandValidationwithNetwork-Integrated Evaluation), which integrates large language model (LLM) text generation with network psychometric methods to automate the early stages of this process. The package generates candidate item pools using LLMs, transforms them into high-dimensional embeddings, and applies a multi-step reduction pipeline — Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), Unique Variable Analysis (UVA), and bootstrap EGA — to produce structurally validated item pools entirely in silico. This tutorial introduces the package across eight parts: installation and setup, text generation, embeddings, item generation, the full AI-GENIE pipeline, the GENIE pipeline for researcher-supplied items, advanced prompt engineering, and fully lo- cal operation. Two running examples illustrate the package’s use: the Big Five personality model (a well-established construct) and AI Anxiety (an emerging construct). The package supports multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, HuggingFace, and local models), offers a fully offline mode with no external API calls, and provides the GENIE() function for researchers who wish to apply the psychometric reduction pipeline to existing item pools regardless of their origin. The AIGENIE package is freely available on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AIGENIE.
